value.body: An advocate represents clients in courts and tribunals. Most start in the chambers of a senior advocate and later build their own practice; some work for government departments or legal aid. A typical day involves court appearances, drafting petitions and replies, meeting clients, and preparing for hearings.

items.label: Typical entry
items.value: LLB (3-year after graduation, or 5-year integrated after Class 12)

items.label: To practise
items.value: Enrol with a State Bar Council and pass the All India Bar Examination (AIBE)

items.label: Where the work is
items.value: District courts, High Courts, tribunals and the Supreme Court

items.label: Advocates enrolled with State Bar Councils
items.source: Ministry of Law & Justice, Rajya Sabha reply

items.label: Advocates on rolls (later estimate)
items.note: Rolls are not fully cleaned of inactive or deceased members
items.source: Ministry of Law & Justice / BCI figures (as reported)

value.title: How you get in
value.body: Complete an LLB from a BCI-recognised college (entry through CLAT, AILET, state law CETs or university tests), enrol with your State Bar Council, and pass AIBE to get a Certificate of Practice. Most freshers then join a senior advocate's chambers as a junior to learn court practice.

value.title: Skills you'll use
items: Drafting petitions, plaints, written statements and applications
Legal research on statutes and case law

value.title: At a glance
items: Early years in litigation often pay little; income tends to build slowly with a client base.
Common paths: own practice, government counsel posts, or judicial service exams.
Advocates can specialise in areas such as civil, criminal, tax or family law.
Building a practice usually takes years of steady work.
